content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

This lesson examines the importance of partnerships between governments, international organizations, private sector entities, and civil society in advancing sustainable energy investments. Learners will explore how collaborative efforts can overcome barriers to financing and create synergies that lead to more successful and scalable renewable energy projects. The lesson also highlights successful case studies of <ai prompt="Tell me more about multi-stakeholder partnerships.">multi-stakeholder partnerships 💬️</ai> that have driven significant progress in the energy sector, with a focus on achieving common goals like energy access, sustainability, and economic development.

concepts.title: multilateral development banks (mdbs)
concepts.body: Multilateral development banks (MDBs) are international financial institutions that provide loans, grants, and technical assistance to support economic development and reduce poverty in developing countries, typically funded by multiple countries.

concepts.title: risk-sharing mechanisms‚àö‚Ñ¢
concepts.body: Risk-sharing mechanisms are strategies or tools used to distribute the financial risks associated with a project or investment among multiple parties, reducing the burden on any single entity.

content.intro: M4: Financing Just Energy Transition | Chapter 5 | Lesson 1 | Part 1
content.title: A: Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs)

content.text:
As mentioned in the previous lesson public-private partnerships 💬️ (PPPs) refer to a range of relationships between public and private actors for a common goal. They are commonly understood to incorporate three key elements.

● Formalized partnership defining the respective roles and responsibilities of public and private actors: There is a spectrum of possible contractual arrangements between public and private entities. These range from relatively short-term service contracts to long-term joint venture arrangements.

● Risk-sharing among public and private actors: PPPs offer a range of risk-sharing mechanisms. They recognize the differing characteristics of public and private actors and seek to optimize the effectiveness of public service delivery by allocating risks to parties most suited to address them.

● Financial reward for private parties, in line with contractual conditions and risk-sharing arrangements: This ensures alignment of interests, motivates performance, and fosters efficiency in achieving common goals.

These elements are captured in the following definition provided by the World Bank: “A long-term contract between a private party and a government agency, for providing a public asset or service, in which the private party bears significant risk and management responsibility.” (World Bank, 2017)

In a broader context, PPPs can be considered as part of the range of policy and financial instruments available to public authorities to “catalyze” or “leverage” private finance. The formal characteristics of PPPs are further valuable to inform effective collaboration between public and private actors.

As discussed earlier, the transition from economic growth to a model of sustainable development necessitates substantial investments in energy transformation. Often the energy infrastructure such as power grids, heating networks and public buildings are owned or controlled by the public and national entities. However, the public sector lacks the financial resources to meet the growing demand for energy investment and government spending and investments have not been sufficient to raise access to renewable (clean) energy in rural areas. This capital shortage problem could be overcome with private investments in the renewable energy sector. However, the total reliance on private sector investments may create a private monopolization of the market in the clean energy sector. Therefore, the PPP model is one of the suggested ways to raise funds for renewable energy project implementation. As a result, the importance of PPP investments in achieving energy efficiency 💬️ and sustainable development goals is being recognized by nations around the world.

PPP investments can play a crucial role in facilitating the expansion of renewable energy capacity. This is primarily due to their ability to provide financial support, foster collaboration, and promote mutual understanding between the private and public sectors.

For instance, PPP investments can cover a wide range of applications and apply to both “short-term management contracts or long-term contracts, including capital, planning contractions, operation, maintenance, and divestment”. The achievement of a balanced risk-sharing mechanism, close monitoring of contract and concessionaire performance, and anticipation of renegotiations are crucial factors that determine the success of PPP projects.

International Financial Institutions (IFIs) offer financial assistance and expert guidance for economic and social development initiatives in recipient nations, aiming to foster international economic collaboration and stability. The term “international financial institution” usually refers to:
and the five main <ai prompt="What is multilateral development banks?">multilateral development banks 💬️</ai> (MDBs):

content.body: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

content.text: The final four of these institutions each concentrate on specific regions and are commonly referred to as regional development banks. The IMF and the World Bank are global organizations with a specialized focus within the UN system but operate independently from it.

IFIs only accept sovereign countries as owner-members. They have a diverse membership that includes both developing countries as borrowers and developed countries as donors. Notably, each of the MDBs also can provide financing to non-sovereign borrowers (i.e. private sector) through their own operations or through dedicated subsidiaries, such as the International Finance Corporation and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency in the case of the World Bank Group. (An exception is the International Finance Corporation, a part of the World Bank Group, which lends to the private sector for approved projects in developing countries.)
MDBs offer financial support for development projects in developing nations through the following means:

content.body: Long-term loans with durations of up to 20 years are determined by prevailing market interest rates. MDBs acquire financial resources for loans by borrowing from international capital markets at low rates and then lending to governments in developing countries.

Very long-term loans with maturities ranging from 30 to 40 years are offered at interest rates significantly lower than market rates. The funding for these comes from direct contributions made by governments in the donor countries and is called concessional finance.
Some MDBs provide grant financing primarily for technical assistance, advisory services, or project preparation.

content.text:
Regional development banks' membership is not typically restricted to countries within the region but includes nations from all over the world. Each IFI operates with its own distinct legal and operational autonomy. However, due to the significant overlap in membership among multiple IFIs, a strong level of collaboration is upheld between them.

Other types of financial institutions also include key actors within the a sustainable financial systems such as central banks, national development banks (NDBs), commercial and investment banks, insurance companies, pension funds, microfinance institutions, and fintech companies.

All these institutions are part of the financial eco-system that is supporting sustainable finance.

content.title: C: The Role of IFIs in financing sustainable energy projects

content.text: Capital Provision and Financial Instruments

IFIs provide various financial products, including long-term loans, concessional finance, and grants, to support clean energy projects.

MDBs like the World Bank Group, African Development Bank, and Asian Development Bank have been instrumental in channeling billions into clean energy initiatives in regions such as Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

Between 2019 and 2022, development finance institutions (DFIs) disbursed an average of $24 billion annually for energy sector projects, with approximately 80% directed toward clean energy .

MDBs mobilize private capital by using concessional loans, risk-sharing mechanisms like guarantees, and co-investment schemes to reduce financial risks. They also invest heavily in improving the creditworthiness of projects, which is critical in countries where traditional financial markets are underdeveloped or where sovereign risks are high.
Risk Mitigation

One of the most important contributions IFIs make to sustainable energy financing is risk mitigation. Institutions such as the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) provide political risk insurance and credit enhancement tools, making it safer for private investors to engage in energy projects in high-risk regions . (See the figure in the next slide).

By doing so, IFIs help lower the cost of capital, particularly for clean energy projects like solar and wind power, which often have high upfront costs but yield long-term returns .

The success of these initiatives depends on reducing financing costs and improving access to global capital markets. Many clean energy technologies, such as solar photovoltaics, require high initial investments, which IFIs help finance through low-interest loans and guarantees, effectively lowering the investment barrier for private sector partners .
Technical Assistance and Capacity Building

Beyond just providing finance, IFIs are heavily involved in offering technical assistance. This support helps EMDE’s build regulatory frameworks and infrastructure conducive to clean energy investment. For example, the World Bank and regional development banks assist countries in drafting policies that promote energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, and more robust project evaluation methods.

content.intro: Latin America and the Caribbean Region
content.title: Case Study: Argentina

content.text:
Argentina is the third-largest electricity power market in Latin America, after Brazil and Mexico. The energy market in Argentina has experienced significant fluctuations, with the country’s energy trade surplus shrinking from USD 3.8 billion in 2006 to a deficit of USD 8.1 billion in 2014 (RELP, RenovAr case study 2024).

Due to structural economic challenges, issues with high energy subsidies, and insufficient investment in energy infrastructure, as well as difficulties accessing international capital markets for infrastructure investment, the renewable energy market had not picked up despite a strong backdrop for developing renewable sources of energy with strong wind, solar, and biomass 💬️ resources. All of that changed in 2015 when Argentina passed Law 27,191 for the Promotion of Renewable Electricity Sources (RE law) (Climate Change Laws, 2025).

Following this, the Ministry of Energy and Mining established an undersecretariat for renewable energy to develop a sustainable energy mandate. The RE law also created a public trust fund called the Fund for the Development of Renewable Energy (FODER) to provide financing and guarantees for renewable generation projects. In early 2016, the government launched the RenovAr initiative, an auction-based renewable energy program aimed at increasing the share of renewable energy production from 8% in 2017 to 16% by 2025, utilizing sources such as wind, solar, biomass, biogas, and small hydropower, in line with its commitment to the Paris Agreement (RELP, RenovAr case study 2024).

content.caption: The two pillars of the RenovAr program are 1) a clear, transparent set of tender rules and 2) long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with a credible guarantee scheme to attract private investment and ensure the financial viability of renewable energy projects (World Bank, 2018). The program is managed by CAMMESA, the country’s wholesale electricity market administrator. The World Bank issued a USD 480 million guarantee to backstop certain government obligations under the program. It later extended this with an additional USD 250 million guarantee to support subsequent auction rounds [be1] (World Bank, 2018). A legal framework was developed for a corporate renewable PPA market, known as ‘MATER’, making it attractive for both local and foreign investors to participate securely in the renewable energy market in Argentina. Understanding the RenovAr guarantee structure

content.text:
All RenovAr projects are structured under a Special Purpose Entity (SPE) with a 20-year PPA term. The tender process outlines clear rules for bidding and project disclosures to meet international standards. There are three levels of guarantees provided under this framework:

The Energy Payment Guarantee is a facility designed to cover any delays or non-payment of energy supplied under the PPA.
The Early Termination Payment Guarantee safeguards the project’s investors against specific political or macroeconomic risks that may materialize. An early termination provision has been structured as a put option of the project’s assets in favor of the SPE.
The Sovereign Default Guarantee has been crafted by the World Bank to partially cover FODER’s obligation to purchase and pay for the project’s assets if the put option is exercised.

In its first three years of operation, the program has held four competitive international public tenders in Argentina (RELP, 2024). Since the launch, a total of 310 wind, solar PV, hydro, and bioenergy 💬️ projects have been awarded. [be1] (RELP, 2024)
 [be1]Reference for this figure?

Key milestones of the scheme include:

2016: Launch of the first round of RenovAr auctions, resulting in the award of over 2.4 GW of renewable energy capacity. The program was oversubscribed six times, indicating strong investor interest. (RELP, 2024)
2017: The World Bank approved a USD 480 million guarantee to support FODER, which facilitates financing for RenovAr projects.
2018: A second World Bank guarantee of USD 250 million was approved to support Round 2 of the RenovAr program, aiming to mobilize private investment representing nine times the value of the guarantee.
2019: The International Finance Corporation (IFC) provided a USD 46.1 million loan for the 88 MW La Genoveva wind project, marking the third project financed by IFC under RenovAr.
2024: As of September, 169 renewable energy projects resulting from RenovAr auctions and MATER were operational, with 50 under construction, totaling USD 11.3 billion in direct investment and 9.1 GW of new-build capacity.
2025: As of January 2025, 175 renewable energy projects from RenovAr auctions are in operation, and 37 are under construction. (RELP,2025).

Role of effective markets in sustainable development

Until 2015, 70% of the cost of electricity generation was borne by the public sector, and private investment did not find the energy market attractive (World Bank, 2018)[be1] . Without an enabling legal and financial framework, it would be extremely hard to attract private capital. The RE law addressed this gap by creating the FODER to facilitate project financing and mitigate liquidity and credit risks.

After gauging investor demand, the World Bank agreed to provide partial guarantees to cover FODER’s obligations, thereby generating investor appetite. As a result, RenovAR, which aimed to attract 1,000 MW worth of new projects, ended up with bids for more than six times that amount (World Bank, 2018). [be2] The program has attracted nearly USD 6 billion in private investment, boosting Argentina’s renewable energy sector and enhancing its attractiveness to international investors (World Bank, 2018).

RenovAr is projected to avoid greenhouse gas emissions of 312 million tons of CO₂ over 20 years, aligning with Argentina’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) commitments under the Paris Agreement. [be3] [po4] The implementation of these projects has also created over 22,000 direct and indirect jobs, contributing to local economic development (RELP, 2025).

Conclusion

The RenovAr program exemplifies a successful public-private partnership model for scaling renewable energy in a developing country. Through strategic financial mechanisms and international collaboration, Argentina has significantly advanced its renewable energy agenda, setting a benchmark for other nations in the region and the world.

takeaways.title: Partnerships are critical in advancing sustainable energy transitions and achieving global climate and development goals. These collaborations involve diverse stakeholders, including governments, international organizations, financial institutions, private sector actors, and civil society

PPPs enable the pooling of public and private resources to finance and implement renewable energy projects. By sharing risks and fostering collaboration, PPPs enhance energy efficiency and expand access to clean energy, particularly in underserved rural areas. Successful PPPs depend on clear agreements, balanced risk-sharing, and incentives that align public and private sector interests.

MDBs play a pivotal role in financing clean energy projects in developing nations through long-term loans, concessional finance, and grants. These institutions also mitigate financial risks by providing guarantees and credit enhancements, making sustainable energy investments more attractive to private sector partners and reducing capital costs for high-upfront projects like solar and wind energy.
